title: Composition over inheritance
problem: A subclass that counts additions to a set reports six after adding three, because the parent's addAll calls the overridden add: the child depends on the parent's internals.
summary: Prefer holding an object and forwarding to it over extending its class: a subclass is coupled to its parent's internals (the fragile base class problem); a wrapper depends only on the contract. Varying behaviour becomes a composed strategy; inheritance stays for true, designed-for subtypes.
catTip: I do not extend Sofa to gain its warmth; I compose with it by sitting on top. When the humans replace the sofa, my behaviour forwards to the new one unchanged.

recall.q: `CountingSet extends HashSet` overrides `add` and `addAll` to count elements, and `addAll` of three elements reports six. What is the problem called, why does it happen, and what is the fix?
recall.a: The fragile base class problem: `HashSet` inherits an `addAll` that calls `add` for each element, so the overridden `add` counts again, and the subclass depends on the parent's undocumented self-use. Fix by composition: hold a `Set` in a field, count in your own methods and forward the rest.

guide.breaks: A subclass inherits its parent's internals as well as its contract, so a parent that calls its own overridable methods, or gains a method in the next release, silently changes what the subclass does.
guide.tradeoffs: Composition costs forwarding boilerplate, an extra object to construct and wire, and one more interface to read, which is pure overhead when the behaviour never varies.
guide.explainSimply: Extending a class is like building your extension on a neighbour's foundation: when they re-lay the floor, your walls crack. Holding the class in a field is like building next door with a corridor between the houses: you only depend on where their front door is. The corridor still breaks if they move the door, but not when they redecorate.
guide.hint: Who calls the overridden add when addAll runs, and whose code does the wrapper version call instead?

meow: Meow does not extend Human to get fed. Meow holds a reference to Human and delegates feeding. Has-a, not is-a.

quiz.prompt: `CountingSet extends HashSet` overrides `add` and `addAll` so that each increments a counter by the number of elements. After `addAll(List.of(1, 2, 3))` the counter is 6. Why?
options: HashSet rejects duplicates, so each element is attempted twice before it is stored
HashSet's inherited addAll calls add for each element, so the overridden add counts each element a second time
Generic type erasure causes the counter to be incremented once per type parameter
addAll is final in HashSet, so the override is ignored and the default behaviour runs
quiz.explanation: The subclass depends on the parent's self-use, an undocumented implementation detail; a wrapper that holds a Set and forwards to it never sees the inner add calls. The duplicates story is believable but wrong: no element here is a duplicate, and HashSet checks membership rather than retrying.

quiz.prompt: In which case is inheritance still the right choice?
options: Two classes share a few utility methods and you want to avoid duplicating them
The subclass is a true subtype and the parent is designed and documented for extension, with its self-use and hook methods specified
The parent class lives in a third-party library whose next version you do not control
The subclass needs to remove a parent method that does not apply to it
quiz.explanation: Inheritance is safe when substitutability holds and the parent promises how it calls its own methods. Shared utilities are the tempting case, but reuse without is-a is exactly what produced Stack extends Vector; removing a method breaks substitutability outright.

cards.q: State the fragile base class problem in one sentence, then name the two fixes.
cards.a: A subclass's correctness depends on undocumented details of how its parent implements its methods (self-use, hooks, methods added later), so a parent change breaks the child without touching it. Fix by holding the parent in a field and forwarding (composition), or by designing and documenting the parent for extension and making everything else final.

cards.q: `Stack extends Vector` in the JDK: what is wrong with it, and how would you design a stack today?
cards.a: A stack is not a vector: callers can insert or remove in the middle and break last-in-first-out. Compose instead: a `Stack` holds a private list and exposes only push, pop and peek, or use `Deque`, which the JDK's own documentation recommends over the Stack class.

sources.title: Joshua Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2018), Item 18 "Favor composition over inheritance" and Item 19 "Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it"
sources.supports: the InstrumentedHashSet/addAll example, the forwarding-class fix, Stack and Properties as JDK violations, and the rule to design for inheritance or prohibit it

sources.title: Java SE 21 API, java.util.AbstractCollection, addAll(Collection)
sources.supports: the documented implementation of addAll, which iterates over the argument and calls add for each element; HashSet inherits it through AbstractSet

sources.supports: Stack extends Vector, and the documentation's recommendation to use Deque instead
